title: RLTF: Reinforcement Learning from Unit Test Feedback
data_curation: Training and evaluation use two existing program-synthesis benchmarks. APPS has 10,000 problems (5k train / 5k test) split into Introductory (3,639), Interview (5,000) and Competition (1,361) difficulties, averaging 23.2 reference programs and 21.2 unit tests per problem with ~20 hidden tests each. MBPP has 974 short single-sentence problems (374 train / 90 val / 500 test / 10 few-shot), each with one ~6.8-line solution and three visible assert-style unit tests. The distinctive data element is the online buffer: instead of pre-collected offline rollouts, the model generates code for sampled problems in real time, runs it through the compiler for unit-test feedback, and stores (problem, generated code, feedback) triples in a fixed-length queue of 6,400 that is refreshed every 50 steps; old samples are evicted as fresh ones arrive, giving on-policy diversity.
curriculum: Not a focus of this paper. The pipeline is a single combined fine-tuning stage on a pretrained code LLM (CodeT5 770M or CodeGen 2.7B): supervised-learning (cross-entropy) and reinforcement-learning losses are summed and optimized together, with half of the training steps devoted to SL and half to RL, mirroring CodeRL's recipe. There is no pretrain->SFT->preference->RL staging, no annealing schedule, and no cross-stage data mixing; the online buffer continuously interleaves freshly generated RL samples with ground-truth SL examples throughout the ~24-hour run.
method: RLTF is an online RL framework for code LLMs that uses multi-granularity unit-test feedback. Two weight-shared LLMs run in parallel: one generates programs and interacts with the compiler to fill an online buffer; the other computes the loss and updates weights. The RL loss is L_rl = -R(W_hat) log P(W_hat|D,theta), with start/end positions (S,E) of the penalized span chosen per feedback type. Three granularities are combined: coarse-grained (whole-episode reward 1.0/-0.3/-0.6/-1.0 for pass/failure/error/syntax-error, as in CodeRL/PPOCoder); fine-grained, which parses compiler error types into U_line (penalize the offending line), U_global (penalize all code for logic errors) and U_ignore (no penalty), using an adaptive weight alpha=(E-S)/T to match magnitudes; and adaptive, with reward -0.3+1.3*N_pass/(N_pass+N_fail). Coarse and adaptive use a dynamic baseline (historical best code). Total loss L_sl+L_coarse+L_fine+L_adaptive. It targets the offline-RL distribution-shift problem and coarse feedback's inability to locate errors.
eval_metrics: Evaluation is on APPS and MBPP using pass@k (k=1,5,10,100,1000) with nucleus sampling (top-p 0.95, temperature 0.6 on APPS, 1.2 on MBPP). Base model is CodeT5 770M (also CodeGen 2.7B). On APPS (all difficulties), CodeT5+RLTF without post-processing reaches pass@1 1.45%, pass@5 3.78%, pass@10 5.21%, pass@1000 19.92%, beating CodeRL (1.32/3.37/17.84) and PPOCoder (1.32/3.37/17.77) and larger GPT/Codex/AlphaCode baselines; with Critic Sampling it reaches pass@1 3.27% and pass@5 7.80%. On MBPP zero-shot, CodeT5+RLTF scores pass@1 71.3, ahead of CodeRL (68.1) and PPOCoder (68.2) and all fine-tuned GPT models up to 137B. Ablations show online+RLTF is best, fine-grained feedback gives the largest gain, and temperature 1.0 outperforms 0.2 or 0.6; RLTF scales better with larger base models (CodeGen 2.7B gains ~1% pass@10).
key_results: CodeT5-770M + RLTF on APPS: pass@1 1.45%, pass@5 3.78%, pass@1000 19.92% (all difficulties), SOTA among CodeT5-based RL methods, beating CodeRL and PPOCoder; with Critic Sampling pass@1 rises to 3.27%. On MBPP zero-shot, CodeT5+RLTF scores pass@1 71.3 vs CodeRL 68.1 and PPOCoder 68.2. Ablation: online framework + RLTF is optimal; fine-grained feedback contributes the largest single gain; benefits grow with base-model size (CodeGen 2.7B gains ~1% pass@10).
evolution_note: RLTF builds on CodeRL (2022) and PPOCoder (2023) by moving code-LLM RL from an offline, coarse-reward regime to an online loop with compiler-parsed, line-level reward shaping -- a 2023 precursor to later execution-feedback / RLVR-style code training that rewards verifiable unit-test signals. Its reliance on hand-crafted Python error categories foreshadows the later need for language-agnostic, automated reward shaping.
